question: Which of the following best defines an agency relationship?
choice_a: A fiduciary relationship in which one party (the agent) is authorized to act on behalf of another (the principal) in dealings with third parties
choice_b: Any relationship in which one person is paid a fee by another for services rendered
choice_c: A relationship that can only be created by a written, notarized contract
choice_d: A partnership in which two parties share equally in the profits of a real estate transaction
explanation: Agency is a common-law fiduciary relationship in which the agent is given authority to act on behalf of, and represent the interests of, the principal in dealings with third parties. It does not require a fee, a partnership, or even a written or notarized document to exist.
source_note: Cornell Law School Legal Information Institute (LII), Wex, 'Agency'; Wikipedia, 'Law of agency' — general common-law doctrine, not Connecticut-specific.

question: A "universal agent" is best described as an agent who
choice_a: Is authorized to handle only one specific transaction, such as the sale of a single house
choice_b: Is empowered to conduct any and all lawful business the principal could personally transact
choice_c: Represents both parties to a transaction with their informed consent
choice_d: Has authority limited to a single geographic market area
explanation: A universal agent has the broadest possible grant of authority, empowered to act for the principal in all matters that may lawfully be delegated. This is the least common form of agency in real estate practice.
source_note: Wikipedia, 'Law of agency' (types of agents: universal, general, special); standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum.

question: A general agent differs from a special agent primarily in that a general agent is authorized to
choice_a: Handle only one isolated, specific act or transaction and nothing more
choice_b: Represent only the buyer in a purchase transaction
choice_c: Conduct a continuing series of transactions or all business of a particular kind for the principal, such as a property manager handling all leasing for an owner's building
choice_d: Bind the principal only after the transaction has already closed
explanation: A general agent has ongoing authority to conduct a particular kind or scope of business for the principal (for example, a property manager authorized to lease, collect rent, and maintain a building), rather than authority limited to one specific transaction, which characterizes a special agent.
source_note: Wikipedia, 'Law of agency'; standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum distinguishing general vs. special agents.

question: Most real estate brokers who list or represent a buyer for a single transaction act in the capacity of a
choice_a: General agent
choice_b: Universal agent
choice_c: Trustee
choice_d: Special agent
explanation: A special agent is authorized to handle a specific, limited transaction or task, such as listing and selling one particular property. Because a typical listing or buyer agency assignment is limited to a single transaction, most real estate agents act as special agents rather than general or universal agents.
source_note: Wikipedia, 'Law of agency' (special agent defined as authorized for specific transactions/tasks only); standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum.

question: A subagent in a real estate transaction is best described as
choice_a: An agent appointed by the original agent to help carry out the agency, who owes the same fiduciary duties to the original principal as the primary agent does
choice_b: A licensee who automatically represents the buyer once the buyer views a listed property
choice_c: An agent who owes fiduciary duties only to the customer they are working with directly
choice_d: Another term for a broker's unlicensed personal assistant
explanation: A subagent is engaged by the original agent (or through cooperative arrangements such as an MLS) to assist in the agency undertaking, but the subagent's fiduciary duties run to the original principal, not to the party the subagent is working with directly. This is precisely why subagency historically created confusion and legal exposure when a subagent worked face-to-face with a buyer while owing duties to the seller.
source_note: Wikipedia, 'Law of agency' (subagency; a subagent's authority derives from the original agent); standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum.

question: Designated agency is a practice that allows a real estate brokerage firm to
choice_a: Assign the same single licensee to fully represent both the buyer and the seller in one transaction
choice_b: Appoint one affiliated licensee to represent the seller and a different affiliated licensee within the same firm to represent the buyer, so each client has undivided representation
choice_c: Avoid ever disclosing agency relationships to either party
choice_d: Allow an unlicensed assistant to close transactions on the broker's behalf
explanation: Designated agency lets a broker name ("designate") specific licensees within the firm to represent the seller and the buyer separately, so that each party receives full, undivided fiduciary representation from their own designated agent, even though both agents share the same supervising broker.
source_note: Standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum on designated agency as an alternative to dual agency; consistent with general agency-law principles on limiting conflicts of interest (Wikipedia, 'Law of agency').

question: Dual agency exists when
choice_a: A broker represents a seller in one transaction and a different, unrelated buyer in a separate transaction
choice_b: Two brokers from different firms each represent one side of the same transaction
choice_c: A single licensee represents both the buyer and the seller in the same transaction
choice_d: An agent temporarily loses their license but continues working under supervision
explanation: Dual agency occurs when one licensee (or, depending on firm policy, one brokerage as a whole) represents both the buyer and the seller in the same transaction, creating an inherent conflict of interest that must be disclosed and consented to.
source_note: Wikipedia, 'Law of agency' ('Agents may represent conflicting principals only after full disclosure and consent'); standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum.

question: Because a dual agent represents both the buyer and the seller in one transaction, which aspect of the traditional fiduciary duties is necessarily limited?
choice_a: The duty to deposit earnest money in a proper account
choice_b: The duty to follow all lawful instructions from every party
choice_c: The duty to disclose known material defects in the property
choice_d: Full, undivided loyalty and complete disclosure of confidential information to either party, since disclosing one party's confidential information would harm the other
explanation: A dual agent cannot give either party undivided loyalty or full disclosure of confidential information (such as a seller's lowest acceptable price or a buyer's highest offer), because doing so for one principal would necessarily breach the duty of confidentiality owed to the other. Dual agents must remain neutral and cannot fully advocate for either side, though duties such as accounting and disclosure of material defects remain intact.
source_note: Wikipedia, 'Law of agency' and 'Fiduciary' (duty of loyalty and confidentiality in conflicted-representation scenarios); standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum on the effects of dual agency.

question: Dual agency is generally lawful only when
choice_a: Both principals have knowledge of the dual representation and give their informed consent
choice_b: Only the seller is informed, since the seller pays the commission
choice_c: The transaction involves commercial rather than residential property
choice_d: The agent verbally promises to favor whichever party contacted them first
explanation: Because dual agency creates an inherent conflict of interest, it is only permissible when both principals are informed of the dual role and knowingly and voluntarily consent to it, typically through a written disclosure and consent form.
source_note: Wikipedia, 'Law of agency' ('Agents may represent conflicting principals only after full disclosure and consent'); standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum.

question: A licensee acting as a "transaction broker" or "facilitator" (nonagent) in a sale
choice_a: Is legally an agent of both parties simultaneously and owes full fiduciary duties to each
choice_b: Assists both the buyer and seller with completing the transaction but does not act as a fiduciary or advocate for either party
choice_c: May only work with buyers, never sellers
choice_d: Cannot receive any compensation for the transaction
explanation: A transaction broker or facilitator is a nonagent who helps bring a willing buyer and willing seller together and assists with the mechanics of closing the deal, but does not represent either party's interests as a fiduciary and cannot advocate for one side over the other.
source_note: Wikipedia, 'Real estate broker' (Florida transaction broker: 'without serving as a fiduciary of any party'); standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum.

question: Even though a nonagent (transaction broker/facilitator) does not owe full fiduciary duties, the licensee must still
choice_a: Keep confidential the seller's lowest acceptable price from the buyer while representing only the seller's interests
choice_b: Advocate exclusively for whichever party is easier to work with
choice_c: Deal honestly and fairly with both parties and properly account for funds and documents entrusted to them
choice_d: Provide the buyer with full fiduciary loyalty identical to that given to a client
explanation: Regardless of agency status, every licensee owes baseline duties of honesty, fair dealing, and proper handling/accounting of trust funds and documents to all parties in a transaction. What a nonagent does not owe is the enhanced fiduciary duties of loyalty, obedience, and confidentiality reserved for a represented client.
source_note: Wikipedia, 'Real estate broker' and 'Law of agency'; standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum on minimum duties owed to all parties.

question: The fiduciary duty of loyalty requires a real estate agent to
choice_a: Recommend the agent's own affiliated title or mortgage company even if it is not in the client's best interest
choice_b: Disclose the principal's confidential negotiating position to any interested third party
choice_c: Follow the principal's instructions even when doing so would violate the law
choice_d: Act solely in the principal's best interest and avoid any conflict of interest or personal gain at the principal's expense
explanation: Loyalty is often described as the most important fiduciary duty: the agent must place the principal's interests above the agent's own and above those of any third party, avoiding undisclosed conflicts of interest or self-dealing.
source_note: Wikipedia, 'Fiduciary' ('the obligation of undivided loyalty'); Cornell LII Wex, 'Fiduciary duty'; standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum (fiduciary duties commonly taught via the mnemonic OLDCAR).

question: The fiduciary duty of obedience obligates an agent to
choice_a: Follow all lawful instructions given by the principal within the scope of the agency agreement
choice_b: Follow any instruction from the principal, even one that violates fair housing or other laws
choice_c: Follow instructions from the customer on the other side of the transaction
choice_d: Disregard the principal's instructions whenever the agent believes a better outcome is possible
explanation: The duty of obedience requires an agent to follow the principal's lawful instructions related to the agency. An agent must never obey an instruction that is illegal, such as one that would violate fair housing law; doing so would not be excused by the duty of obedience.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'Fiduciary duty' (duty of obedience); standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum.

question: The fiduciary duty of disclosure requires an agent to
choice_a: Reveal the principal's confidential motivations to the opposing party
choice_b: Disclose to the principal all information relevant to the transaction that could affect the principal's decisions, such as offers received or facts about a prospective buyer's ability to perform
choice_c: Disclose the agent's personal opinions about unrelated properties on the market
choice_d: Withhold all offers below full asking price from the principal
explanation: The duty of disclosure requires an agent to keep the principal fully informed of all facts and developments material to the transaction, including every offer received and any relevant information about the parties involved, so the principal can make informed decisions.
source_note: Wikipedia, 'Law of agency' (principal must receive 'full disclosure of all information relevant to the transactions,' applied reciprocally to what an agent must relay); standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum.

question: The fiduciary duty of confidentiality generally requires an agent to
choice_a: Share the principal's negotiating strategy with cooperating agents to speed up the transaction
choice_b: Keep confidential information private only while the listing agreement remains active, with no obligation once it terminates
choice_c: Keep the principal's confidential information, such as their motivation or lowest acceptable price, private from third parties, and this duty typically continues even after the agency relationship ends
choice_d: Disclose confidential principal information whenever a customer asks directly
explanation: Confidentiality protects information the principal would not want disclosed, such as their true motivation or price flexibility. Unlike most other fiduciary duties, the duty of confidentiality is generally recognized as surviving termination of the agency relationship, meaning the agent must continue to protect that information even after the agency ends.
source_note: Wikipedia, 'Law of agency' (respecting principal's confidentiality) and 'Fiduciary' (disclosure/confidentiality obligations); standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum noting confidentiality's survival past termination.

question: The fiduciary duty of accounting requires an agent to
choice_a: Provide the principal with a written appraisal of the property's value
choice_b: File the principal's income tax return related to the sale proceeds
choice_c: Refuse to accept any funds on behalf of either party
choice_d: Keep accurate records of, and be able to produce upon request, all funds, documents, and property (such as an earnest money deposit) entrusted to the agent during the transaction
explanation: The duty of accounting requires the agent to properly handle, safeguard, and maintain accurate records of all money and property received on behalf of others in the transaction, and to report and account for those items promptly and accurately.
source_note: Wikipedia, 'Fiduciary' ('maintain records...provide full accounting'); standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum (accounting duty in earnest money handling).

question: The fiduciary duty of reasonable care and diligence (skill) requires an agent to
choice_a: Exercise the degree of skill and care that a reasonably competent real estate professional would use, including researching and disclosing material facts and advising the principal competently
choice_b: Guarantee that the property will sell for the exact listing price
choice_c: Personally perform all appraisal, inspection, and legal work on every transaction
choice_d: Avoid giving the principal any advice so as to remain neutral
explanation: The duty of reasonable care and diligence obligates the agent to bring professional-level competence, skill, and effort to the representation, including conducting reasonable investigation into material facts and providing informed advice, though it does not make the agent a guarantor of a particular outcome.
source_note: Wikipedia, 'Fiduciary' (duty of care: 'act on an informed basis after due consideration'); standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum.

question: An express agency relationship is created when
choice_a: A third party simply assumes an agency exists based on rumor
choice_b: The principal and agent explicitly agree, whether orally or in writing, to establish the agency, such as by signing a listing agreement
choice_c: The agent unilaterally decides to represent someone without that person's knowledge
choice_d: A court orders the relationship into existence after a dispute arises
explanation: Express agency arises from a direct, stated agreement between principal and agent, whether oral or written, that establishes who the agent will represent and the scope of the agent's authority. In real estate, this is typically documented through a listing agreement or buyer representation agreement.
source_note: Wikipedia, 'Law of agency' (express agreement as a method of creating agency); standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum.

question: An implied agency may be found to exist when
choice_a: A written listing agreement has been fully executed by both parties
choice_b: A court formally appoints an agent by decree
choice_c: The words and conduct of the parties indicate an intention to create an agency relationship, even though no explicit agreement was signed
choice_d: The agent has passed the state licensing examination
explanation: Implied agency can be created through the conduct and communications of the parties, such as a broker consistently acting on someone's behalf with that person's knowledge and acquiescence, even absent an express written or oral agreement.
source_note: Wikipedia, 'Law of agency' (implied authority/creation based on conduct); standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum.

question: Agency by ratification occurs when
choice_a: A principal signs a buyer representation agreement before any showings occur
choice_b: A licensee's real estate license is renewed by the state licensing board
choice_c: Two brokers agree in advance to split a commission
choice_d: A principal accepts and approves after the fact the previously unauthorized acts of someone who acted as if they were the principal's agent
explanation: Ratification allows a principal to retroactively approve an act performed by someone without prior authority to act as their agent, either expressly or through conduct that shows acceptance of the unauthorized act, thereby creating the agency relationship after the fact.
source_note: Wikipedia, 'Law of agency' (ratification: 'principal acceptance of previously unauthorized acts'); standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum.

question: Agency by estoppel arises when
choice_a: A principal's words or conduct lead a third party to reasonably believe an agency relationship exists, and the third party relies on that belief to their detriment, preventing the principal from later denying the agency
choice_b: A licensee's authority is automatically revoked for failing to pay license renewal fees
choice_c: A written agency agreement is notarized by a title company
choice_d: The principal formally fires the agent in writing
explanation: Agency by estoppel does not require an actual agreement between principal and agent; rather, it arises because the principal's own conduct created a reasonable appearance of authority on which a third party justifiably relied, so the principal is legally estopped (prevented) from denying that the agency existed.
source_note: Wikipedia, 'Law of agency' ('agency by estoppel' where principals are 'estopped from denying the grant of authority'); standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum.

question: A listing agreement is best understood as
choice_a: A deed transferring an ownership interest in the property to the broker
choice_b: An employment contract that also establishes an agency relationship between the seller (principal) and the broker (agent), authorizing the broker to market the property
choice_c: A guarantee by the broker that the property will sell within a set time
choice_d: A contract solely between the seller and the eventual buyer
explanation: A listing agreement is simultaneously an employment contract (setting compensation and terms of service) and an express agency agreement, giving the broker authority to represent the seller's interests in marketing and negotiating the sale of the property.
source_note: Wikipedia, 'Real estate broker' (listing agreements referenced as agency-creating documents); standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum.

question: A buyer agency (buyer representation) agreement establishes
choice_a: A relationship in which the buyer becomes the broker's employee
choice_b: An arrangement that automatically makes the broker a dual agent
choice_c: An agency relationship in which the broker represents the buyer as principal and owes the buyer the traditional fiduciary duties
choice_d: A guarantee that the buyer will purchase a specific property
explanation: A buyer representation agreement is the buyer-side counterpart to a listing agreement: it creates an express agency in which the broker represents the buyer's interests and owes the buyer fiduciary duties such as loyalty, obedience, and confidentiality.
source_note: Wikipedia, 'Real estate broker' (buyer representation agreements referenced as agency-creating documents); standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum.

question: Which statement about agency and compensation is most accurate?
choice_a: Whoever pays the commission automatically becomes the party the broker represents
choice_b: A buyer's agent cannot be paid through the seller's proceeds under any circumstances
choice_c: Compensation may never be shared between a listing broker and a buyer's broker
choice_d: A broker's fiduciary duty runs to the party the broker has agreed to represent, regardless of which party ultimately pays the commission
explanation: The source of compensation does not determine who the agent represents. For example, a buyer's agent may still be compensated out of the seller's proceeds through a cooperating (offer of) commission, yet the agent still owes fiduciary duties exclusively to the buyer, not the seller.
source_note: Standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum addressing the common misconception that payment source determines agency; consistent with general agency-law principle that agency status turns on representation, not payment (Wikipedia, 'Law of agency').

question: General agency disclosure practice requires a licensee to
choice_a: Disclose to consumers, as soon as practicable, which party the licensee represents (or that the licensee represents no one) before eliciting confidential information
choice_b: Wait until closing to reveal which party the licensee represented
choice_c: Disclose agency status only if the consumer specifically asks
choice_d: Provide agency disclosure only in commercial transactions, never residential
explanation: A core purpose of agency disclosure is to ensure consumers understand, early in their dealings with a licensee, whether that licensee represents them, the other party, or no one, before the consumer shares information they might otherwise expect to remain confidential.
source_note: Wikipedia, 'Real estate broker' ('licensees must disclose to prospective buyers and sellers the nature of their relationship'); standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum.

question: Even though a real estate licensee owes no fiduciary duties to a customer (an unrepresented party), the licensee must still
choice_a: Advocate for the customer's negotiating position against the licensee's own client
choice_b: Treat the customer honestly and deal with them fairly, avoiding fraud and misrepresentation
choice_c: Disclose the client's confidential motivations to the customer
choice_d: Refuse to answer any factual questions the customer asks
explanation: All real estate licensees, regardless of who they represent, owe non-represented customers a baseline duty of honesty and fair dealing. This falls short of full fiduciary loyalty and advocacy, which are reserved for the licensee's own client.
source_note: Wikipedia, 'Real estate broker' and 'Law of agency'; standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum on minimum duties owed to third parties/customers.

question: Regardless of which party a real estate agent represents, the agent generally must disclose to all parties to the transaction
choice_a: The client's confidential settlement authority
choice_b: The agent's personal commission split with their broker
choice_c: Known material or latent defects that affect the property's value, desirability, or safety
choice_d: Other unrelated properties currently for sale in the area
explanation: The duty to disclose known material or latent defects runs to all parties in a transaction, not just to the agent's own client, because withholding known facts that affect the property's value or safety could constitute misrepresentation or fraud regardless of agency status.
source_note: Standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum on material fact disclosure to all parties, consistent with general fiduciary/agency-law prohibitions on fraud (Wikipedia, 'Fiduciary').

question: An agent's statement describing a home as a "dream house" or "won't last long" is generally considered
choice_a: Fraud, because any exaggerated statement about a property is illegal
choice_b: A breach of fiduciary duty owed to the customer
choice_c: Illegal steering under fair housing law
choice_d: Permissible sales talk ("puffing"), not an actionable misrepresentation, since it is an opinion rather than a statement of material fact
explanation: "Puffing" refers to subjective, exaggerated statements of opinion (such as calling a home a "dream house") that a reasonable person would not take as a statement of objective fact. It is distinguished from misrepresentation, which involves a false statement of material fact that a party relies upon to their detriment.
source_note: Standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum distinguishing puffing from actionable misrepresentation; consistent with general fraud/misrepresentation doctrine (Cornell LII Wex, 'Fiduciary duty').

question: The duty to properly account for and safeguard a customer's earnest money deposit
choice_a: Applies to both clients and customers, since safekeeping of trust funds is a basic duty owed to all parties in a transaction, not only to a represented client
choice_b: Applies only when the customer is also the agent's client
choice_c: Does not apply if the transaction ultimately falls through
choice_d: Is waived automatically in a dual agency transaction
explanation: Proper handling and accounting for trust funds, such as earnest money, is a fundamental duty owed to everyone involved in a transaction, regardless of whether the person is the agent's client or merely a customer, because these funds belong to someone other than the agent or broker.
source_note: Wikipedia, 'Fiduciary' (accounting obligations); standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum on trust fund handling as a universal duty.

question: An agent who deliberately limits the neighborhoods shown to a homebuyer based on the buyer's race or national origin has violated
choice_a: Only the duty of loyalty owed exclusively to the agent's seller-client
choice_b: The duty of honest and fair dealing owed to all parties, in addition to violating fair housing law
choice_c: No agency-related duty, since fair housing law is unrelated to agency principles
choice_d: Only the duty of accounting
explanation: Steering a customer or client toward or away from neighborhoods based on a protected class is both a fair housing violation and a breach of the basic duty of honest, fair, and equal treatment owed to every party a licensee deals with, regardless of representation status.
source_note: Standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum linking fair housing obligations to the general duty of honesty and fair dealing owed to all parties.

question: An agency relationship established for a defined term, such as a six-month listing agreement, generally terminates by
choice_a: Automatic renewal unless the principal objects in writing
choice_b: Operation of law only if the property fails to sell
choice_c: Expiration of the agreed-upon time period
choice_d: Immediate termination the moment the first offer is rejected
explanation: When an agency agreement specifies a fixed term, the agency automatically ends when that term expires, unless the parties agree in advance to renew or extend it.
source_note: Standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum on termination of agency by expiration of term; consistent with general agency-law termination doctrine (Wikipedia, 'Law of agency').

question: When a broker successfully procures a ready, willing, and able buyer and the resulting sale closes, the listing agency relationship ends by
choice_a: Renunciation by the agent
choice_b: Operation of law
choice_c: Mutual rescission
choice_d: Completion (fulfillment) of the purpose of the agency
explanation: An agency created for a specific purpose, such as selling a particular property, naturally terminates once that purpose has been fully accomplished, for example when the closing occurs and the sale is complete.
source_note: Standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum on termination by completion/performance of the agency's purpose; consistent with general agency-law doctrine.

question: A principal and an agent may end their agency relationship at any point before its natural conclusion by
choice_a: Mutual agreement (mutual rescission) of both parties
choice_b: The principal's silence alone, with no communication to the agent
choice_c: A unilateral decision that requires no notice and creates no possible liability
choice_d: The passage of any amount of time, regardless of the agreement's stated term
explanation: Because agency is a consensual relationship, the principal and agent can always agree together to terminate it early through mutual agreement or rescission, releasing both parties from further obligations under the agreement.
source_note: Standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum on termination by mutual agreement; consistent with general agency-law doctrine (Wikipedia, 'Law of agency').

question: If a principal revokes an agent's authority before the end of an agreed-upon term without legal cause, the principal
choice_a: Faces no possible consequences, since a principal may always revoke an agent's authority freely and without cost
choice_b: May still be liable to the agent for damages or breach of contract, even though the agent's actual authority is effectively terminated
choice_c: Is automatically required to pay the agent's full expected commission regardless of any contract terms
choice_d: Cannot revoke the agency under any circumstances once it has been created
explanation: A principal generally retains the power to revoke an agent's authority at any time, but revoking it without legal cause before the end of an agreed term may still constitute a breach of the underlying agency contract, exposing the principal to liability for damages even though the agency itself ends.
source_note: Wikipedia, 'Law of agency' (principals generally may terminate, but for fixed-period agencies must compensate the agent absent 'sufficient cause'); standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum.

question: When an agent unilaterally withdraws from the agency relationship before completing the assigned task, without justification, this is known as
choice_a: Ratification
choice_b: Estoppel
choice_c: Renunciation, which may expose the agent to liability for breach of the agency agreement
choice_d: Apparent authority
explanation: Renunciation occurs when the agent, rather than the principal, chooses to end the agency relationship before fulfilling its purpose. Like an unjustified revocation by the principal, an unjustified renunciation by the agent can create liability for breach of the agency contract.
source_note: Wikipedia, 'Law of agency' (agent renunciation as an act-of-parties termination method); standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum.

question: The death or adjudicated incapacity of either the principal or the agent generally
choice_a: Has no effect on the agency relationship, which continues with the deceased or incapacitated party's estate
choice_b: Only terminates the agency if the other party files a lawsuit
choice_c: Converts the agency into a general agency automatically
choice_d: Terminates the agency relationship automatically, by operation of law
explanation: Because agency depends on the legal capacity and continued existence of both parties, the death or legal incapacity of either the principal or the agent automatically terminates the agency relationship by operation of law, without any further action required.
source_note: Wikipedia, 'Law of agency' (termination by operation of law: 'Death of either party,' 'Insanity of either party'); standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum.

question: If the property that is the subject of a listing agreement is completely destroyed (for example, by fire) before it is sold, the agency relationship
choice_a: Terminates by operation of law because the subject matter of the agency no longer exists
choice_b: Continues in full force, with the agent now obligated to sell the vacant lot at the original price
choice_c: Automatically converts to a property management agreement
choice_d: Remains valid only if the destruction was caused by the principal
explanation: When the specific subject matter of an agency, such as a particular structure, is destroyed or otherwise ceases to exist, the agency terminates by operation of law because it is no longer possible to carry out the original purpose of the agreement.
source_note: Standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum on termination by destruction of the subject property; consistent with general agency-law termination principles (Wikipedia, 'Law of agency').

question: Which of the following, occurring during the agency term, would terminate the agency relationship by operation of law?
choice_a: A temporary decline in the local real estate market
choice_b: Bankruptcy of the principal
choice_c: The agent taking a scheduled vacation
choice_d: A buyer submitting a lowball offer that the principal rejects
explanation: Bankruptcy or insolvency of the principal (or agent) is a recognized ground for automatic termination of an agency by operation of law, since it may affect the principal's legal capacity to have the agent act on their behalf. Market fluctuations, a rejected offer, or an agent's temporary absence do not, by themselves, terminate the agency.
source_note: Wikipedia, 'Law of agency' (termination by operation of law: 'Bankruptcy/insolvency of either party'); standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum.

question: When a principal terminates the primary agency relationship with the original agent, any subagents appointed under that agency
choice_a: Automatically become the principal's new direct agents with independent authority
choice_b: Retain full authority to continue acting on the principal's behalf indefinitely
choice_c: Also have their authority terminated, since a subagent's authority derives from and cannot exceed the authority of the original agent
choice_d: Are converted into buyer's agents by default
explanation: Because a subagent's authority is derived entirely from the original agent's authority, terminating the original agency relationship also ends the authority of any subagents appointed to help carry it out.
source_note: Wikipedia, 'Law of agency' ('Termination affects subagents as well'); standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum.

question: "Apparent authority" refers to a situation in which
choice_a: An agent has express written authority signed by the principal
choice_b: A court grants authority to an agent after a lawsuit
choice_c: An agent's license has been suspended by the state real estate commission
choice_d: A third party reasonably believes, based on the principal's words or conduct, that a person has authority to act as the principal's agent, even though no actual authority was granted
explanation: Apparent (or "ostensible") authority arises from the principal's conduct or representations that would lead a reasonable third party to believe an agency relationship and corresponding authority exist, regardless of whether actual authority was ever granted between principal and agent.
source_note: Wikipedia, 'Law of agency' (apparent/ostensible authority defined); Cornell LII Wex, 'Agency.'

question: Under the doctrine of vicarious liability in agency law, a principal may be held legally responsible for
choice_a: The tortious (wrongful) acts of an agent committed within the scope of the agent's authorized duties
choice_b: Every action the agent takes in the agent's purely personal life, unrelated to the agency
choice_c: Criminal acts committed by the agent decades before the agency relationship began
choice_d: Nothing, since agents are always personally and solely liable for their own conduct
explanation: Vicarious liability holds a principal responsible for an agent's wrongful acts committed within the scope of the agency, on the theory that the agent was acting on the principal's behalf; this liability generally does not extend to acts clearly outside the scope of the agent's duties.
source_note: Cornell LII Wex, 'Agency' (principal liability for agent torts committed during official duties; the 'frolic or detour' distinction); Wikipedia, 'Law of agency.'

question: In real estate practice, the key distinction between a "client" and a "customer" is that
choice_a: A client always pays a commission, while a customer never does
choice_b: A client is a party the licensee represents in an agency relationship and is owed full fiduciary duties, while a customer is a party the licensee assists but does not represent, owed only basic honesty and fair dealing
choice_c: A customer is legally entitled to the same fiduciary duties as a client
choice_d: There is no meaningful legal distinction between the two terms
explanation: "Client" designates the party in an agency relationship with the licensee, entitled to the full range of fiduciary duties (loyalty, obedience, disclosure, confidentiality, accounting, and reasonable care). "Customer" designates a non-represented party the licensee still deals with honestly and fairly, but without fiduciary obligations.
source_note: Standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum distinguishing client and customer terminology; consistent with general agency/fiduciary-law principles (Wikipedia, 'Law of agency').

question: A brokerage firm that practices exclusively "single agency" is one that
choice_a: Represents both parties in every transaction through a single designated agent
choice_b: Only handles single-family residential properties, never commercial listings
choice_c: Represents only one party, either the buyer or the seller, in any given transaction, and never both
choice_d: Employs only one licensed agent at the entire firm
explanation: A single agency policy means the firm commits to representing only one side of any transaction, either the buyer or the seller, avoiding dual agency (and, depending on firm policy, sometimes avoiding designated agency as well) so that undivided loyalty to one party is always maintained.
source_note: Standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum on single agency as a firm-level policy contrasted with dual/designated agency.
